panels.what:
BuiltWright in one paragraph
BuiltWright is a set of 21 linked reference and troubleshooting modules for industrial maintenance, written by a Red Seal millwright, that runs on any phone, tablet, or computer, online or offline, from a single folder of files. Each module explains how a class of equipment works, how it fails, how to diagnose it from the symptom, what to change so it does not fail again, how to work on it safely, and includes a self-check for training. A symptom-first hub routes any fault to the right module, a search covers everything, a reference module holds the tables and calculators, a PM task library is derived from every diagnostic result, and a root cause report form closes the loop. It is built for the maintenance department that wants its technicians to find causes, not swap parts.
What it is not
  • Not a CMMS. It does not hold work orders, inventory, or schedules. It holds knowledge and gives a technician a place to think.
  • Not a substitute for the manufacturer's manual. Every module says so: the manual and the drawing govern the numbers. BuiltWright teaches what the numbers mean and what to do when the manual is not to hand.
  • Not a certification. The self-checks are for learning, not for proving competence to a regulator.
  • Not a replacement for lockout training, confined space training, or any plant program. It reinforces them from the machine side.
  • Not connected to anything. Nothing a technician types leaves the device. The PM library ticks and the root cause form live in the browser on that device.

panels.deploy:
Deploying it in a plant
  • Host the folder. Any web server that can serve static files: the plant intranet, a shared drive with a web front end, or a hosting service. All the files in one folder, unchanged. README_hosting.txt has the notes. Opening the hub file directly from a shared drive also works for reading; the offline install needs a web address.
  • Use https if you can. Offline mode and the home screen install only work over https (or on the technician's own computer). On plain http the pages still work; they just need a connection.
  • Put the hub on the phones. Each technician opens the hub address once, adds it to the home screen, and from then on it opens like an app and works in the parts of the plant with no signal.
  • Put the hub on the shop computer. A bookmark, and the search page open on a second tab.
  • Print what needs printing. Any tab prints cleanly in black and white. The Safety tabs, the reference tables, and the commissioning checklist are the ones that end up in binders.
  • Updates. Replace the files in the folder. The service worker version number in sw.js is bumped with each release so installed phones fetch the new files on their next connection.
  • Custom content. Plant-specific numbers (your grease quantities, your alignment tolerances, your set points) belong in your equipment records and PM sheets, which the modules tell technicians to consult. A facility mode that overlays your specifics on the modules is the next stage of the product.
panels.program:
A twelve-week program for a new maintenance technician
One module a week, about two hours of reading and self-check, plus a supervised walk on a real machine that uses that module. The walk is the point; the reading is preparation for it. Adjust the order to the plant: a plant that is all conveyors moves week 11 to week 3.
WeekModuleThe walk
114 Machine Safeguarding and PSR (Hazards, Guards, Safety tabs) plus every module's Safety tab as a skimWalk a machine and list its nip, crush, shear, and entanglement points and how each is guarded. Do a lockout with the supervisor watching.
221 Precision MeasurementMeasure a shaft seat at four positions with a micrometer and a bore with a bore gauge; write it all down; compare to the drawing.
302 Bearing FailureOpen the failed-parts shelf; read three bearings and name the mechanism. Grease a bearing by formula with the relief plug out.
405 Lubrication SystemsWalk the lube room; match every product to its application list; take an oil sample the right way.
503 Couplings and AlignmentSoft foot check and a full alignment on a spare pump set or a training rig, readings recorded.
608 Power TransmissionTension a belt drive by deflection gauge; gauge a sheave; measure a chain for elongation.
701 Pump SystemsWalk a pump's system chain from supply to discharge; find the gauges; explain what each reading means.
806 PneumaticsTrace a pneumatic circuit from compressor to cylinder on a machine; find every FRL and drain; do a leak listen with the screwdriver.
910 Motors: Mechanical SideRead three nameplates; infrared a running motor at both ends; do the instant-off test; write a handoff package for a real fault.
1009 GearboxesInspection cover off a locked-out gearbox; photograph the teeth; measure backlash.
1115 Conveyors (or 07 Hydraulics, 17 Fans, 18 Compressors, depending on the plant)Walk a conveyor running from outside the guards; chalk the belt edge; identify the take-up type and where it sits.
1216 Root CauseTake one repeat failure from the plant's history and write a root cause report using the form, with the supervisor. Present it.
After twelve weeks the technician has walked twelve machines with a purpose, written one root cause report, and worked every self-check in the modules that matter most. The remaining modules (04, 07, 11, 12, 13, 17 through 20) are read as the work brings them up, and the hub routes to them from the symptom.
panels.using:
Using the tools as a manager
PM Task Library
  • Open it by component. Every task says which fault it prevents and links to the diagnosis. Tick the ones your PM already does. What is left unticked is the gap between your PM program and the failures the series knows about.
  • Set the interval per task for your plant. Export to CSV and merge into the CMMS. The interval column is a suggestion from the wording; your equipment history governs.
  • When a technician asks why a task is on the sheet, the answer is the link. Put the link in the CMMS task description.
Root Cause report
  • Make it the standard for any repeat failure, any failure over a cost threshold, and any injury or near miss. The form fits on a phone and prints on one page.
  • Review each report for a chain that ends at a person. Send those back. The Traps tab explains why.
  • Every corrective action gets an owner and a date, and the report stays open until the verification date passes and the failure has not returned.
Self-Check
  • Assign a module. Ask for the self-check to be worked through with the reasons read. Then walk the machine with the technician and ask them the questions in their own words. The score on the screen is not the measure; the conversation at the machine is.
  • Scores are not stored anywhere. That is deliberate: it is a learning tool, not a surveillance tool, and technicians use it more when it is not a test.
Safeguarding and PSR
  • Before a new machine or a modification, the Safeguarding module's PSR tab tells you whether Regulation 851 section 7 applies and what the engineer will need. Doing the millwright homework before the engineer arrives is the difference between an afternoon and a week.
  • The Hazards and Guards tabs are the reference for building and reviewing guards to CSA Z432.
panels.measure:
Measuring whether it is working
MeasureHowWhat good looks like after a year
Repeat failure rateFailures on the same machine and component within 12 months, from the CMMSFalling. This is the one that matters.
Root cause reports completedCount, and the share that reach a system cause with an owner and a dateEvery repeat and every costly failure has one; most reach a system cause.
PM tasks with quantities and settingsAudit the PM sheets: does "grease" have a quantity, does "align" have a tolerance, does "tension" have a numberYes on every sheet.
Commissioning baselinesMachines installed or rebuilt this year with vibration, temperature, alignment, and amps recorded on day oneAll of them.
Failed parts readShare of failed-part work orders that name a mechanismMost of them.
Electrical handoffsMotor faults that arrive at the electrician with amps, temperatures, and the solo run result written downAll of them, and the electrician says so.
Guards found offWeekly walk countZero, and when one is found, the design reason is fixed.
Self-checks workedAsk. It is not logged.Every technician has done the modules for the machines they own.
None of these needs new software. They come out of the CMMS and a weekly walk. A department that tracks the first one and the third one will see the rest follow.
Field tip for managers: the shelf and the whiteboardTwo things cost nothing and change a department. A shelf where every failed part sits for a month with the work order number on its box. A whiteboard with the machines that have failed twice this year. The shelf is evidence; the whiteboard is the priority list. BuiltWright is what the technician reads standing in front of either one.
